coherence.reasons: Both run the same sound chain: market growth is not profit, unit economics are negative, customers do not repay, cash breaches the floor, software is the better path. X's summary maps cleanly onto its five sections and each title is backed by a calculation. Y adds an explicit hypothesis tree (six conditions the launch needs) that orders the whole deck, and its governing claim that software reaches profitability within current cash is backed by a cash model. X's equivalent claim rests only on a '13.7 months until the floor, if new contracts cut the burn' caveat. Y has one internal flaw: the slide 7 sensitivity chart mislabels its bars (riders shown as +0.22 and orders/day as −0.31, when my recomputation gives the reverse), which contradicts its own correct title and text. Y is still slightly tighter overall.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion (R1: do not launch, grow software) and both reject a one-store pilot for sound reasons (little new learning, breaches runway). Y weighs the alternatives more fully. It scores three options against explicit criteria tied to the investors' two constraints. It tests whether the recommended option itself meets 'profitability within current cash' (break-even about month 26 at 60% growth, month 36 at 40%, minimum 34%). It names the main risk to its own recommendation and mitigates it with tranche-released hires and a 90-day checkpoint. It also addresses the first-mover risk and tells the board not to extend the pop-up. X's recommendation is defensible and its reopen conditions are quantified ($50.37 AOV, 27.1% retention), but it never shows the software path reaching profitability, only that it stays above the floor for 13.7 months if nothing improves.

evidence.reasons: Both hit every required calculation: −$6.17, −$1.76, −$12.57, +$2.02, runway of $2.5M or about 6 months against 12, CAGR 41.5%, and Zipcart moves on the median site at −$1.05. X's numbers all check out ($63.36 break-even AOV, 14.4 orders per rider-hour, 14.8-month payback, 1.3x, $18.2M), with few unsupported claims; 'did not rely on running stores more efficiently' is a mild overreach. Y uses the critical evidence more deeply. It derives the Zipcart break-even density (about 1,042 orders a day) and concedes a profitable route may exist at high density with premium pricing, which is the engagement the key asks for in K9. It adds a single-driver sensitivity on the plan, a scale sanity check ($266M GMV against QuickBasket's $210M), the pop-up ramp estimate, the rider-pay impact (+$1.48 per order) and a best-observed payback of 113 months. Against that, Y's slide 7 chart has the rider and density values swapped, and its software cash model rests on a constructed, flat cost base, though that is disclosed and stress-tested. Y's better use of evidence slightly outweighs X's cleaner record.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis on the right grounds and avoid the traps (growth as justification, density as a fix, promotion-fuelled growth, ignoring runway). Y handles the hypothesis more explicitly and more fairly. It states the hypothesis, breaks it into six conditions and tests each. It directly tests the founders' capability claim ('we run stores better than anyone') against the pop-up falling below the median on all four drivers, while granting the fair caveat that the pop-up was early and ramping. On Zipcart it concedes that a profitable route may exist at top-quartile density with a fee, then turns that into a re-entry trigger. X confirms the 40% growth claim and shows the plan exceeds the best observed site on all four drivers, but treats Zipcart mostly as a rebuttal ('profit came from charging more') and does not address the capability claim head-on.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the board to the right decision with correct core numbers. X is leaner and has no numerical slips. Y serves the decision better because it shows the recommended alternative actually satisfies the investors' constraints: a cash model with a break-even month, a 34% minimum growth threshold and phased hires. It also gives the founders' evidence a fair hearing, sets observable re-entry triggers and a 90-day checkpoint, and discloses its judgement calls on ambiguous inputs. Y's mislabelled sensitivity chart and its constructed software cost base are real weaknesses, but neither changes the conclusion.
